lesson.title: TH→D Discrimination Drills
lesson.subtitle: Which d-words hardened from th — and which are D→T doubles running in reverse?

hook.title: Two D's, Two Directions
hook.content: German d comes from two different ancestors. One kind was always English th: thin → dünn, thorn → Dorn, thumb → Daumen, thirst → Durst, thing → Ding. The other kind was English d that German pushed forward to t: door → Tür, day → Tag. So when you meet a German d-word, run both checks: does swapping d for th reveal an English word (Durst → thirst)? Or is the d the original, with the real story hiding in a t somewhere? Direction is the whole game.

footnotes.title: The Chain Explains the Crowding
footnotes.content: TH moved onto D's old street (think → denken), so D had to move to T's street (door → Tür). That chain is why both languages can't use the same sounds for the same words — everyone moved house at once.

pattern.title: Run Both Checks
pattern.content: Check one — the th-swap: dünn (thin), dick (thick), Dorn (thorn), Daumen (thumb), Durst (thirst), Ding (thing), Erde (earth), drei (three). Check two — the reverse: if the d looks original, look for a t: Tür pairs with door through D → T (the German word kept the ancient vowel but the shift went the other way), Tag with day. Beware the lookalikes: dick does not mean its English sound-alike — it means thick; das Ding means thing, and English kept the Germanic sense in 'the whole thing' and even the old assemblies called 'Things'.
pattern.linguist_note: Earth → Erde runs the same dental hardening as three → drei; English's th here is the ancient fricative þ, which High German hardened to d while English kept it spelled th into modern times.

exercises.prompt: Separate the true TH→D words — match each to its English twin:
exercises.explanation: Swap the d for th and the English word appears — these are hardened dental fricatives.

exercises.prompt: Which shift connects English 'door' and German 'Tür'?
exercises.meaning: door ↔ Tür runs D → T, not TH → D
exercises.explanation: Tür's t is the hardened English d — the chain move. The th-swap check fails here; the t tells the real story.

exercises.prompt: What English word is the twin of 'Dorn'?
exercises.explanation: Dorn hardened the th; the rose's spike is the same Germanic word on both shores.
earth → Erde: the ancient þ hardened to d, exactly as in three → drei.

exercises.idea: you're describing a skinny thing to a friend: the thing is thin
cues: Both words carry the shift: thing → Ding, thin → dünn (TH → D, twice in one sentence)
The thing is neuter: das Ding
After ist the adjective stays bare and goes last: das Ding ist dünn

vocab_hints.note: das Ding — neuter, like English 'the thing'

exercises.explanation: Two TH→D words in one sentence, built from your own thought: das Ding and dünn.

summary.outcome: Distinguish TH→D words (dünn, Dorn, Durst) from D→T reverses (Tür, Tag) and use both in sentences.
summary.takeaway: German d has two ancestors: swap d for th to find one kind, look for the t to catch the other.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: the sibilant shift from the other side — t becomes s, ss and z: water becomes Wasser, two becomes zwei.

twist.explanation: Re-assembling "Das Ding ist dünn" from scratch locks in the structural pattern of TH→D Discrimination Drills without relying on short-term echo.

daumen.context_translation: I press my thumbs (I cross my fingers for you).

durst.context_translation: I have great thirst / I am very thirsty.

tür.etymology_derivation: d → t with vowel mutation to ü.

tag.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and y → g.

bad.etymology_derivation: Final th shifted to d (devoiced in pronunciation to [t]). Verb: baden (to bathe).

teil.etymology_derivation: d → t (cognate with English "deal" as in a great deal / dole).

seltsam.etymology_derivation: Middle High German seltsām, built with the suffix -sam, which the page glosses as English -some; English seldom is listed as a cognate, German having hardened d to t in the root seld-. [wiktionary]

moos.context_phrase: Das Moos wächst auf dem Stein.
moos.context_translation: The moss grows on the stone.
moos.etymology_derivation: From Old High German mos, from Proto-Germanic *musą. English moss is the cognate from the same Proto-Germanic word. [wiktionary]

mittags.context_translation: At midday we eat a hot meal.
mittags.etymology_derivation: Mittag + adverbial -s — literally at midday; Mittag is the structural twin of English midday. [wiktionary]

werktag.context_phrase: An Werktagen stehen wir früh auf.
werktag.context_translation: On workdays we get up early.
werktag.etymology_derivation: Werk + Tag — the exact structural twin of workday; Werk is the twin of work (k → ch) and Tag the twin of day (d → t). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
